"What motivated me to join the program is that I was deeply interested in space technology. I was in this country so I could work on space technology. NASA called for applications to become scientist-astronauts and that is as close as you can get to space technology," said Chapman iframe with ABC News' (Australia) Weekend Magazine.
After undergoing basic astronaut training, including spending more than a year learning how to fly NASA's T-38 supersonic training jets at Randolph Air Force Base in Texas, Chapman was assigned to support roles for the then underway Apollo moon landings. Most notably, he served as mission scientist for Apollo 14, which would land Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell on the lunar surface while Stu Roosa remained in orbit in 1971.
"I'm not in charge of them, I am coordinating them," Chapman said of the Apollo 14 science experiments and his role as mission scientist, iframe at the time. "I am acting as the liaison between the experimenters and the crew."

    had received his Ph.D. at MIT in instrumentation, with a focus on general relativity. Going on to become a scientist-astronaut, he was on the
    lookout for gravity experiments to conduct in space and consulted
    Weiss, who had been on his thesis committee. “We were going to the
    Moon, NASA had plenty of money, and anything seemed possible,”
    recalls Chapman of that era. Weiss told Chapman about his idea to use
    laser interferometry to search for gravity waves. Chapman himself had
    been thinking of approaches other than bars. Enthused by the prospect and looking for further collaborators in industry, he then talked
    to Forward, who was continuing his bar work at Hughes. (He had
    three small bars operating up and down the coast of California, one of
    them in his bedroom closet.) “Phil Chapman put me on to Weiss’s
    interferometer idea,” says Forward, resurrecting the notion he first
    heard from Weber years earlier. The possibility of a future NASA
    project got both Forward and Weiss working on the idea independently.

# Rocket carrying late Nasa astronaut’s remains explodes over New Mexico

## 

Rocket’s payload also included science experiments part of Nasa’s TechRise Student Challenge

Vishwam Sankaran Thursday 04 May 2023 06:31 BST

  *   * Bookmark

A rocket carrying the cremated remains of a late Nasa astronaut exploded seconds after launch over the New Mexico desert.

The small suborbital rocket by Colorado-based company UP Aerospace was carrying student experiment payloads for Nasa as well as the cremated remains of astronaut Philip K Chapman who died in April 2021 and chemist Louise Ann O’Deen, among others, Gizmodo reported.

Dr Chapman was a radio physicist, selected as a scientist-astronaut by NASA in August 1967.

He was involved in preparations for Nasa’s Moon missions, serving as scientist for the Apollo 14 mission, the American space agency noted.

On Monday, just seconds after liftoff, the UP Aerospace rocket carrying Dr Chapman’s cremated remains suffered an anomaly and was destroyed in flight, according to local news.

During his time at NASA, he worked as a mission scientist for Apollo 14, contributing heavily to the mission’s accomplishment of putting men on the moon.

Chapman claimed he was the man behind one of the mission’s most famous televised moments, encouraging the Apollo 14 astronauts to test famous astronomer Galileo Galilei’s theory that a feather and a hammer would fall at equal speed in a vacuum.

PROMOTED CONTENT

Chapman never got his chance to travel to space, although he continued to work in the private sector of commercial spaceflight for many years.

Chapman regretted missing the opportunity to go to space. Speaking to author Colin Burgess about his book Shattered Dreams: The Lost and Cancelled Space Missions, Chapman said: “The Skylab in which I had hoped to live is now a tourist attraction … I sometimes visit it when I am in Washington but it is very sad to see it wasted.”

A small capsule containing Chapman’s ashes will be launched into orbit aboard a Celestis spaceflight on 30 November.

# Rocket carrying late Nasa astronaut’s remains explodes over New Mexico

## 

Rocket’s payload also included science experiments part of Nasa’s TechRise Student Challenge

Vishwam Sankaran Thursday 04 May 2023 06:31 BST

  *   * Bookmark

A rocket carrying the cremated remains of a late Nasa astronaut exploded seconds after launch over the New Mexico desert.

The small suborbital rocket by Colorado-based company UP Aerospace was carrying student experiment payloads for Nasa as well as the cremated remains of astronaut Philip K Chapman who died in April 2021 and chemist Louise Ann O’Deen, among others, Gizmodo reported.

Dr Chapman was a radio physicist, selected as a scientist-astronaut by NASA in August 1967.

He was involved in preparations for Nasa’s Moon missions, serving as scientist for the Apollo 14 mission, the American space agency noted.

On Monday, just seconds after liftoff, the UP Aerospace rocket carrying Dr Chapman’s cremated remains suffered an anomaly and was destroyed in flight, according to local news.

# Rocket carrying late Nasa astronaut’s remains explodes over New Mexico

## 

Rocket’s payload also included science experiments part of Nasa’s TechRise Student Challenge

Vishwam Sankaran Thursday 04 May 2023 06:31 BST

  *   * Bookmark

A rocket carrying the cremated remains of a late Nasa astronaut exploded seconds after launch over the New Mexico desert.

The small suborbital rocket by Colorado-based company UP Aerospace was carrying student experiment payloads for Nasa as well as the cremated remains of astronaut Philip K Chapman who died in April 2021 and chemist Louise Ann O’Deen, among others, Gizmodo reported.

Dr Chapman was a radio physicist, selected as a scientist-astronaut by NASA in August 1967.

He was involved in preparations for Nasa’s Moon missions, serving as scientist for the Apollo 14 mission, the American space agency noted.

On Monday, just seconds after liftoff, the UP Aerospace rocket carrying Dr Chapman’s cremated remains suffered an anomaly and was destroyed in flight, according to local news.

L185: 
L186: The small suborbital rocket by  -based company UP Aerospace was carrying student experiment payloads for Nasa as well as the cremated remains of astronaut Philip K Chapman who died in April 2021 and chemist Louise Ann O’Deen, among others, Gizmodo reported.
L187: Dr Chapman was a radio physicist, selected as a scientist-astronaut by NASA in August 1967.
L188: 
L189: He was involved in preparations for Nasa’s Moon missions, serving as scientist for the Apollo 14 mission, the American space agency noted.
L190: 
L191: On Monday, just seconds after liftoff, the UP Aerospace rocket carrying Dr Chapman’s cremated remains suffered an anomaly and was destroyed in flight, according to local news.
L192: The rocket was packed with 13 payloads, including a series of student science experiments as part of Nasa’s TechRise Student Challenge as well as cremated human remains of various people from Celestis, a company that specialises in space memorial services.
L193: 
L194: While the rocket was destroyed after liftoff, the Celestis payload “was unharmed and will be able to be relaunched”, the company noted. The remains were sent off by families wishing for a memorial service in space for their departed members.
L195: “We are reviewing the details and the video with UP Aerospace. As soon as we have clearance from them about the details and the video itself, we will share all of that information with families via email,” it tweeted.
L196: 
L197: “All 120 flight capsules are safely in the hands of launch personnel and will be returned to us awaiting our next flight as soon as UP and Spaceport America complete their investigation and any required fixes are implemented,” Celestis chief Charles Chafer said in a statement.
L198: Nasa noted in a statement on Tuesday that it would work with the TechRise project administrator and UP Aerospace to determine potential paths forward for the affected student payloads.
L199: 
L200: “We look forward to working with UP Aerospace to return to flying payloads and experimental technologies on future flights,” Christopher Baker, programme executive in Nasa’s Space Technology Mission Directorate, said.
L201: “While this is obviously a disappointing outcome for today’s flight, that should not diminish the work it took to get here. Each of these TechRise student teams should be proud of their accomplishment in delivering an experiment for launch and we will be working on future opportunities for them to see their experiments in space,” Mr Baker said.

L13: ## Packet containing Chris Boshuizen's name patch from Blue Origin spaceflight NS-18
L14: This name patch is part of a collection of items related to the Blue Origin NS-18 spaceflight which took place on 13 October 2021, with Australian engineer Dr Chris Boshuizen as a member of the crew. The patch, along with the Australian flag patch and toy koala are all accompanied by space-flown certificates confirming their authenticity.
L15: The koala was one of a small number of items chosen by Boshuizen to take on the flight with him, while the flag and name patches were souvenired from his capsule seat following the successful flight. Also included is an official NS-18 mission patch, and a mission-style patch depicting Australia on the globe.
L16: Blue Origin is one of a number of privately-funded space organisations founded by wealthy tech entrepreneurs from around the early 2000s, and represents a shift in the paradigm of space exploration (sometimes referred to as Space 2.0), which up until that time had been dominated by large Government-funded organisations such as NASA.
L17: Such organisations are also notable for leading the development of reusable rocket boosters (traditionally always single-use) as well as for re-exciting the public about space exploration through their celebrity flights, headline-grabbing stunts and the promise of making space travel accessible to the general public in the near future. Dr Chris Boshuizen is an Australian engineer who was one of four passengers ('tourists') aboard the Blue Origin NS-18 suborbital spaceflight on 13 October 2021.
L18: In doing so, Boshuizen become only the third Australian ever to fly to space (after Paul Scully-Power and Andy Thomas in the 1980s) – and the first to do so as an Australian citizen. The flight is perhaps most famous for including 'Star Trek' actor William Shatner.
L19:      L20: ### Summary
L21: 
L22: #### Object Statement
L23: 
L24: Name patch and certificate, from seat capsule, on Blue Origin spaceflight NS-18, fabric / paper / plastic / foil, made by or for Blue Origin LLC, owned by Dr Chris Boshuizen, flown from Van Horn, Texas, USA, 13 October 2021
L25: #### Physical Description
L26: 
L27: Small, rectangular, mission-style patch embroidered with the name 'C. Boshuizen'. The patch is accompanied by a small 'Certificate of Flight', and both are sealed together in a plastic and foil packaging, to remain unopened.

L45: ### HISTORY
L46: #### Notes
L47: This patch was attached to Dr Chris Boshuizen's capsule seat aboard the Blue Origin NS-18 spaceflight on 13 October 2021, and souvenired by Boshuizen (with permission) following the flight. Boshuizen is an Australian engineer who grew up in the small town of Tumbarumba, in New South Wales, Australia.
L48: Boshuizen always dreamed of travelling into space and had originally intended to join the Australian Defence Force Academy (ADFA) after completing his schooling, planning to become a pilot with the Air Force, and to find a way to the USA, and ultimately the NASA astronaut program, from there. While attempting to enrol with ADFA, Boshuizen discovered he was colourblind, causing him to be rejected by the Academy, but quickly resolved that he would find another way into space.
L49: Boshuizen completed a Bachelor of Science (in Physics and Mathematics) at the University of Sydney in 1999, and then a PhD in astronomy and space physics in 2005 (also at the University of Sydney), where his thesis project focused on the development of a small space telescope designed to measure the oscillations of stars (a field known as asteroseismology).
L50: After completing his studies, Boshuizen become the executive director of the Space Generation Advisory Council (a global, non-profit organisation and network which aims to represent young space professionals and university students to the United Nations, space agencies, industry, and academia), from 2006-2008.
L51: Following that, Boshuizen took up a position at NASA Ames Research Center, where he worked on various projects, including the Lunar Atmosphere Dust Environment Explorer, a low-cost robotic lunar exploration and technology demonstration mission, and PhoneSat, a 10cm (1U) cube satellite built from off-the-shelf electronics.
L52: Boshuizen has described the success of the PhoneSat project as significant in helping to change the attitudes of the space industry, and proving that it was possible to put working satellites into orbit at very low cost. In 2010, Boshuizen co-founded Planet Labs, a company that used low-cost cubesats to capture satellite imagery of Earth. Boshuizen's co-founders were Will Marshall and Robbie Schingler, whom he had first met at the World Space Congress in 2002, when the trio were still school students.
L53: Marshall and Boshuizen had worked together at NASA Ames on the PhoneSat project, while Schingler was previously the chief of staff in NASA's Office of the Chief Technologist. Notably, Planet Labs helped to provide information to emergency services, to help with the distribution of resources, following the earthquake that affected Nepal in 2015. This was another significant moment for Boshuizen, whose ethos is that space should be for all, and benefit all.
L54: In 2015, Boshuizen left Planet Labs, after 5 years as the chief technology officer, to become a partner in DCVC, a venture capital firm based in San Francisco, USA, where he helps to fund start-ups that share his goal of democratising access to space. On 13 October 2021, Boshuizen fulfilled his childhood dream of flying to space, as a passenger aboard the Blue Origin NS-18 suborbital spaceflight.
L55: This was achieved after many months of campaigning the Blue Origin team to include him on one of their early flights. In doing so, Boshuizen become only the third Australian ever to fly to space (after Paul Scully-Power and Andy Thomas in the 1980s) – and the first to do so as an Australian citizen (Philip K Chapman was the first Australian-born astronaut, training with NASA in the 1970s, but never flew in space).

During his time at NASA, he worked as a mission scientist for Apollo 14, contributing heavily to the mission’s accomplishment of putting men on the moon.

Chapman claimed he was the man behind one of the mission’s most famous televised moments, encouraging the Apollo 14 astronauts to test famous astronomer Galileo Galilei’s theory that a feather and a hammer would fall at equal speed in a vacuum.

PROMOTED CONTENT

Chapman never got his chance to travel to space, although he continued to work in the private sector of commercial spaceflight for many years.

Chapman regretted missing the opportunity to go to space. Speaking to author Colin Burgess about his book Shattered Dreams: The Lost and Cancelled Space Missions, Chapman said: “The Skylab in which I had hoped to live is now a tourist attraction … I sometimes visit it when I am in Washington but it is very sad to see it wasted.”

A small capsule containing Chapman’s ashes will be launched into orbit aboard a Celestis spaceflight on 30 November.
